audioBrief.headline: The Bab el-Mandeb Bottleneck: How Maritime Conflict Reordered Global Supply Chains
audioBrief.script: Good day. The maritime chokepoints of the Middle East have transformed commercial shipping into an endurance test. Over twelve percent of global seaborne trade has diverted around the southern tip of Africa, adding ten to fourteen transit days and billions in fuel burn. The NZZ analyzes the geopolitical realignments and macroeconomic inflation risks threatening European consumer markets. For the Neue Zürcher Zeitung, Zurich.

slides.headline: Three Structural Consequences for Europe
slides.bodyText: The protracted crisis has transformed European supply-chain resilience from a theoretical ideal into an urgent balance-sheet liability.

dialecticalFaq.topic: Maritime Security and the Red Sea Crisis

items.question: Can naval convoys guarantee safe passage through the strait?
items.answer: Naval task forces can intercept the majority of inbound aerial and surface threats, but commercial hull underwriters refuse risk coverage as long as residual strike probabilities remain above zero.

items.question: Why not absorb the Cape detour as the permanent new baseline?
items.answer: The Cape detour consumes approximately 9% of global container fleet capacity simply through longer voyage durations, reducing ship availability and artificially elevating worldwide freight costs.

items.question: What structural resolution does the NZZ recommend?
items.answer: A coordinated European naval presence combined with long-term port infrastructure diversification and sovereign manufacturing buffers, reducing unilateral dependency on vulnerable single-point transit canals.
